title: 6 Critical First-Week-Of-School Strategies For Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2019/07/27/first-week-of-school-strategies-difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out six first-week strategies specifically for a class's most challenging students, arguing this window is a rare chance to set a positive trajectory before a failed dynamic sets in by October. Recommendations include treating difficult students exactly like the rest of the class rather than singling them out, assuming they are capable of meeting expectations, withholding excessive or condescending praise, enforcing consequences quickly and then moving on without lecturing, letting rapport build naturally rather than forcing it, and avoiding prolonged personal conversations that can end up excusing misbehavior. He closes by framing this counterintuitive, unlabeling approach as simple but genuinely transformative for at-risk students.
points: Recommends treating difficult students as ordinary members of the class rather than giving them extra attention or check-ins, which he frames as a subtle form of labeling.
Advises assuming difficult students can meet expectations, arguing this shifts subconscious teacher behavior and begins to rebuild their self-image.
Calls for withholding excessive praise for expected behavior since difficult students read it as condescending or as evidence they're seen as incapable.
Urges enforcing consequences quickly and walking away without lectures or pep-talks, preserving students' dignity to reflect independently.
Warns against extended personal conversations that can inadvertently excuse poor behavior, favoring instead simple, consistent belief in the student.
quotes: Focusing on difficult students, checking in on them, using proximity with them, and otherwise spending more time with them than your other students are all forms of labeling.
When you treat challenging students like everyone else, they tend to behave like everyone else.
Difficult students have been praised so often and for so long that it’s lost all its meaning.
Never tiptoe around difficult students or be fearful of holding them accountable. These, too, are labeling behaviors that can also give them a sense of entitlement.
You can build strong rapport with difficult students by just allowing them to enjoy being a regular student.
In most cases, difficult students don’t need a counselor. They need a leader and role model who sees their worth and potential and treats them as if they really can do it.
